Surat al-Fath is Madinan by consensus, and it has twenty-nine verses. It was revealed at night between Makkah and Madinah concerning the event of al-Hudaybiyah. Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from al-Zuhri, from Urwah, from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and Marwan ibn al-Hakam, who said: "Surat al-Fath was revealed between Makkah and Madinah concerning the event of al-Hudaybiyah, from its beginning to its end." In the two Sahihs, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was traveling on some of his journeys, and Umar ibn al-Khattab was traveling with him at night. Umar asked him about something, but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not answer him. Then he asked again and he did not answer him, then he asked a third time and he did not answer him. So Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "May Umar's mother be bereaved! You pressed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ three times, and each time he did not answer you." Umar said: "So I urged my camel forward and went ahead of the people, and I feared that a Qur'an might be revealed concerning me. I had not waited long before I heard a crier calling me, so I said: 'I feared that a Qur'an had been revealed concerning me.' So I went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, greeted him, and he said: 'There has been revealed to me tonight a surah that is dearer to me than everything the sun rises upon,' then he recited: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear victory.'" This is the wording of al-Bukhari. Al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a hasan, gharib, sahih hadith." In Sahih Muslim, from Qatadah, that Anas ibn Malik related to them, saying: "When there was revealed: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest, that Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins, complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path, and that Allah may support you with a mighty support' [48:1–3], on his return from al-Hudaybiyah, while the people were overcome by sorrow and dejection, and he had slaughtered the sacrificial animals at al-Hudaybiyah, he said: 'There has been revealed to me a verse that is dearer to me than the whole world.'" Atha related from Ibn Abbas: The Jews reviled the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims when there was revealed the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9]. They said: "How can we follow a man who does not know what will be done with him?" This weighed heavily upon the Prophet ﷺ, so Allah the Exalted revealed: "Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest, that Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins." Muqatil ibn Sulayman said similarly: When there was revealed the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9], the polytheists and the hypocrites rejoiced and said: "How can we follow a man who does not know what will be done with him or with his companions?" So after he returned from al-Hudaybiyah there was revealed: "Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest," meaning: We have decreed for you a decree. This verse abrogated that one. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There has been revealed to me a surah that would not please me to have red camels in exchange for it." Al-Mas'udi said: "It has reached me that whoever recites Surat al-Fath on the first night of Ramadan in voluntary prayer, Allah will preserve him that year."

﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest﴾ (1)

It has been differed concerning what this conquest is. In al-Bukhari: Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to me, saying: Ghundar related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, saying: I heard Qatadah from Anas concerning "Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest," he said: "Al-Hudaybiyah." Jabir said: "We did not count the conquest of Makkah except as the day of al-Hudaybiyah." Al-Farra' [in the Tafsir of al-Tabari: "al-Bara'"] said: You count the conquest as the conquest of Makkah, and the conquest of Makkah was indeed a conquest, but we count the conquest as the Pledge of Ridwan on the day of al-Hudaybiyah. We were with the Prophet ﷺ fourteen hundred [in al-Tabari: "five hundred"], and al-Hudaybiyah is a well. Al-Dahhak said: "Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest" without fighting, and the treaty was part of the conquest. Mujahid said: It is his sacrifice at al-Hudaybiyah and his shaving of his head. He said: The conquest of al-Hudaybiyah was a great sign: its water was drawn out, he spat into it, and it gushed with water until all who were with him drank. Musa ibn Uqbah said: A man said at their departure from al-Hudaybiyah: "This is not a conquest; they have barred us from the House." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Rather, it is the greatest of conquests. The polytheists have consented to repel you from their lands with peace, to ask you for a settlement, to seek security from you, and they have seen from you what they disliked." Al-Sha'bi said concerning the saying of Allah the Exalted "Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest": "It is the conquest of al-Hudaybiyah. He obtained there what he had not obtained in any campaign. Allah forgave him his earlier and later sins, the Pledge of Ridwan was made, the people were fed from the palm groves of Khaybar, the sacrificial animal reached its place, and the Romans prevailed over the Persians, so the believers rejoiced at the victory of the People of the Book over the Magians." Al-Zuhri said: "al-Hudaybiyah was the greatest of conquests, for the Prophet ﷺ came to it with one thousand four hundred. When the treaty was concluded, people mingled with one another, learned, and heard about Allah, so no one desired Islam except that he attained it. Those two years had not passed before the Muslims came to Makkah with ten thousand." Mujahid also said, and al-Awfi: It is the conquest of Khaybar. The first view is more common, and Khaybar was only a promise they were given, as will be explained in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The bedouins who stayed behind will say when you set out﴾ [in this surah, verse 15] [al-Fath: 10], and His saying: ﴿Allah promised you much booty that you will take, and He hastened this for you﴾ [in this surah, verse 20] [al-Fath: 20]. Mujammi' ibn Jariyah, who was one of the reciters who recited the Qur'an, said: "We witnessed al-Hudaybiyah with the Prophet ﷺ. When we turned away from it, people were urging on their camels, so some people said to others: 'What is the matter with the people?' They said: 'Allah has revealed to the Prophet ﷺ.' He said: So we set out hastening, and we found the Prophet of Allah ﷺ at Kura' al-Ghamim, and when the people gathered, the Prophet ﷺ recited: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest.' Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'Is it a conquest, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes, by Him in whose hand my soul is, it is indeed a conquest.' So Khaybar was divided among the people of al-Hudaybiyah, and no one entered it except those who had witnessed al-Hudaybiyah." It has been said: The saying of Allah the Exalted "a conquest" indicates that Makkah was conquered by force, because the term "conquest" is not applied absolutely except to what was conquered by force; this is the true meaning of the term. It may be said: "The town was conquered by treaty," but the treaty is not understood except when it is joined to the conquest, so the conquest in a treaty becomes figurative. The reports indicate that it was conquered by force, and the discussion of this has already passed [see vol. 8, p. 2], and will come.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "a manifest victory" is incomplete, because His saying "that Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin" is connected to the victory. It is as if He said: "We have granted you a manifest victory so that Allah may combine for you, with the victory, forgiveness, and so that Allah may thereby gather for you what gladdens your eye in this world and the Hereafter." Abu Hatim al-Sijistani said that the lam here is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam). This is an error, because the lam of oath is not vowelled with a kasra and does not govern a subjunctive verb. If this were permitted, one could say *liyaqum Zaydun* (so that Zayd stands), interpreting it as *liyaqumanna Zaydun* (Zayd will surely stand).

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask how the conquest of Mecca was made a cause of forgiveness? I answer: it was not made a cause of forgiveness, but rather for the gathering of the four matters enumerated, namely: forgiveness, the completion of His blessing, the guidance to the straight path, and the mighty victory. It is as if He said: "We facilitated for you the conquest of Mecca and gave you victory over your enemy, so that there might be gathered for you the honour of both abodes and the benefits of the immediate and the deferred." It is also permissible that the conquest of Mecca, insofar as it was a struggle (jihad) against the enemy, was a cause of forgiveness and reward.

In al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Anas, who said: "The verse, 'That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what follows,' was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) on his return from al-Hudaybiyah. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'There has been revealed to me a verse that is dearer to me than everything upon the earth.' Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to them. They said: 'Congratulations, O Messenger of Allah! Allah has made clear what He will do with you; so what will He do with us?' Then there was revealed to him: 'That He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow...' up to '...a great triumph.'" He said: this is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (good and sound). And there is also a report on the authority of Majma' ibn Jariyah.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of "that Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what follows." It was said: "what preceded of your sin" refers to what was before the prophethood, and "what follows" refers to what came after it. This was said by Mujahid. Similar was said by al-Tabari and Sufyan al-Thawri. Al-Tabari said: this refers back to His statement, exalted is He: "When the help of Allah comes and the victory..." up to "...oft-returning" (Q. 110:1–3). "That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin" refers to what was before the prophethood, "and what follows" refers to up to the time of the revelation of this verse.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "what preceded of your sin" refers to what you did in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah) before it was revealed to you. "And what follows" refers to everything you did not do. This was also said by al-Wahidi. The discussion of the occurrence of minor sins (saghā'ir) in the case of the prophets has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah. This is one view.

It was also said: "what preceded" refers to what was before the conquest, and "what follows" refers to what came after the conquest. It was said: "what preceded" refers to what was before the revelation of this verse, and "what follows" refers to what came after it.

ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasani said: "what preceded of your sin" means the sin of your two parents, Adam and Eve, and "what follows" means the sins of your community (ummah). It was said: it means the sin of your father Ibrahim, and "what follows" means the sins of the prophets.

It was said: "what preceded" refers to the sin of the Day of Badr, and "what follows" refers to the sin of the Day of Hunayn. The preceding sin on the Day of Badr was that he began to supplicate and say: "O Allah, if You destroy this band (of believers), You will never be worshipped on earth." He kept repeating this statement several times, so Allah revealed to him: "From where do you know that if I destroy this band, I shall never be worshipped?" So this was the preceding sin. As for the following sin, it was on the Day of Hunayn: when the people were routed, he said to his paternal uncle al-ʿAbbas and his cousin Abu Sufyan: "Hand me a handful of pebbles from the valley." They handed it to him, and he took it in his hand and threw it into the faces of the polytheists, saying: "Ugly are the faces. Ḥm. They will not be helped." So the people fled to the last man, and none remained but his eyes were filled with sand and pebbles. Then he called out to his companions, and they returned. He said to them when they returned: "If I had not thrown them, they would not have fled." So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: "And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw" (Q. 8:17). This was the following sin.

Abu ʿAli al-Rudhbari said: He says, "If you had any sin, old or recent, We would have forgiven it for you."

"As-sakinah" (tranquility): stillness and calm. Ibn 'Abbas said: every "sakinah" in the Qur'an means tranquility (tuma'ninah), except the one in al-Baqarah [[see vol. 3, p. (248)]]. The meaning of the increase of faith was already discussed in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. (280)]]. Ibn 'Abbas also said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was sent with the testimony that there is no god but Allah. When they affirmed it, he enjoined upon them prayer (salah); when they affirmed that, he enjoined upon them zakat; when they affirmed that, he enjoined upon them fasting; when they affirmed that, he enjoined upon them hajj. Then He perfected their religion for them. This is His saying: ﴿that they may increase in faith along with their faith﴾, meaning, affirmation of the laws of faith along with their affirmation of faith. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: fear (khashyah) along with their fear. Al-Dahhak said: certainty (yaqin) along with their certainty. ﴿And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the angels, the jinn, the devils, and mankind. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of the conditions of His creation, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He wills.

[Qur'an 48:5] "That He may admit the believing men and believing women to gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein eternally, and remove from them their misdeeds. And that is, in the sight of Allah, a great achievement."

That is: He sent down the tranquility (sakinah) so that they would increase in faith. Then that increase is by means of their being admitted to Paradise.

"And that was" means: that promise, of entering Makkah and the forgiveness of sins.

"In the sight of Allah a great achievement" means: deliverance from every distress and attainment of every desired thing.

When he recited "and guide you to a straight path," [it was revealed concerning the community: "and guide you to a straight path"] (Qur'an 48:20) [Qur'an 48:2]. And when he said, "and Allah will help you with a mighty help" (Qur'an 48:3), there was revealed [Qur'an 30:47] "And it was ever incumbent upon Us to help the believers."

"Those who think evil thoughts about Allah" means: they thought that the Prophet ﷺ would not return to Madinah, nor would any of his companions when he set out for al-Hudaybiyah, and that the polytheists would wipe them out. As He said: ﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again﴾ [al-Fath: 12]. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: "as-sau'" here means corruption. ﴿Upon them is a circle of evil﴾: in this world, by killing, capture and taking captive, and in the Hereafter, Jahannam. Al-Jawhari said: sā'ahu yasū'uhu sau'an (with a fatha) and masā'atan and masāyatan, the opposite of sarrahu, and the noun as-sau' (with a damma). It was also read "ʿalayhim dā'iratu as-Su'" meaning defeat and harm. Whoever reads with a fatha, it is from al-masā'ah (displeasure). ﴿And Allah was angry with them, and cursed them, and prepared for them Jahannam, and evil is it as a destination. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verses 8–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾. Qatadah said: a witness over your ummah concerning the delivering (of the message). It was also said: a witness over them concerning their deeds, whether obedience or disobedience. It was also said: a bringer of clarity to them concerning what We sent you with to them. It was also said: a witness over them on the Day of Resurrection. So he is a witness to their actions today, and a witness against them on the Day of Resurrection. This meaning has already been explained in "al-Nisa'" from Sa'id ibn Jubayr [[Note: what was previously mentioned in Surah al-Nisa' is Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. See vol. 5, p. 197 onward.]]. ﴿And a bearer of good news﴾ to those who obey him, with Paradise; ﴿and a warner﴾ from the Fire to those who disobey. This was said by Qatadah and others. The derivation and meanings of "bearer of good news" (bashārah) and "warning" (nidhārah) have already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, pp. 184, 238, second or third edition.]]. The words "witness," "bearer of good news," and "warner" are in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of anticipation (ḥāl muqaddarah). Sibawayh related: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow." The meaning is: We have sent you, (being) those who determine by your testimony on the Day of Resurrection. Upon this you say: "I saw ʿAmr standing tomorrow."

﴿That you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu ʿAmr read "liyu'minu" with the yā' (third person), and likewise "yuʿazziruhu, wa-yuwaqqiruhu, wa-yusabbiḥuhu," all with the yā' as narration. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this because the believers are mentioned before and after it: before it is "li-yudkhila" and after it is ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. The rest read with the tā' as address, and Abu Hatim preferred this.

﴿And honor him﴾: i.e., you magnify him and exalt him; said by al-Hasan and al-Kalbi. Ta'zir means magnifying and esteeming. Qatadah said: you help him and protect him from (harm). From this comes ta'zir in the hadd (prescribed punishment), because it prevents (the offense). The poet al-Qutami said:

Alā bakarat Mayy bi-ghayri safāhatin... tuʿātibu wa-l-mawdūdu yanfaʿuhu al-ʿazr

Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrimah said: you fight alongside him with the sword. Some scholars of language said: you obey him. ﴿And revere him﴾: i.e., you make him master (of your affairs); said by al-Suddi. It was also said: you magnify him. Tawqir means magnifying and adorning as well. The pronouns in both (verbs) refer to the Prophet ﹙ﷺ﹚. Here is a complete pause, then you begin with ﴿and glorify Him﴾, i.e., glorify Allah, ﴿morning and evening﴾, i.e., in the evening. It was also said: all the pronouns refer to Allah, the Exalted. According to this, the interpretation of "you honor Him and revere Him" is: you affirm for Him the validity of lordship and negate that He has a son or a partner. Al-Qushayri preferred this view. The first view is the opinion of al-Dahhak, and according to it some of the speech refers to Allah, glorified and exalted, namely "and glorify Him," without any disagreement, and some of it refers to His Messenger ﷺ, namely "and honor him and revere him," i.e., you address him by his prophethood and messengership, not by his name or kunyah. Regarding "and glorify Him" there are two views: first, glorifying Him by declaring Him free of every imperfection; second, it is the performance of the prayer in which there is tasbih. ﴿Morning and evening﴾, i.e., at dawn and at dusk. This has already been discussed. The poet said:

La-ʿamrī la-anta al-bayt ukrimu ahlahu... wa-ajlisu fī afyā'ihi bi-l-aṣāʾil

(The verse is by Abu Dhu'ayb.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verses 8–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾. Qatadah said: a witness over your ummah concerning the delivering (of the message). It was also said: a witness over them concerning their deeds, whether obedience or disobedience. It was also said: a bringer of clarity to them concerning what We sent you with to them. It was also said: a witness over them on the Day of Resurrection. So he is a witness to their actions today, and a witness against them on the Day of Resurrection. This meaning has already been explained in "al-Nisa'" from Sa'id ibn Jubayr [[Note: what was previously mentioned in Surah al-Nisa' is Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. See vol. 5, p. 197 onward.]]. ﴿And a bearer of good news﴾ to those who obey him, with Paradise; ﴿and a warner﴾ from the Fire to those who disobey. This was said by Qatadah and others. The derivation and meanings of "bearer of good news" (bashārah) and "warning" (nidhārah) have already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, pp. 184, 238, second or third edition.]]. The words "witness," "bearer of good news," and "warner" are in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of anticipation (ḥāl muqaddarah). Sibawayh related: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow." The meaning is: We have sent you, (being) those who determine by your testimony on the Day of Resurrection. Upon this you say: "I saw ʿAmr standing tomorrow."

﴿That you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu ʿAmr read "liyu'minu" with the yā' (third person), and likewise "yuʿazziruhu, wa-yuwaqqiruhu, wa-yusabbiḥuhu," all with the yā' as narration. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this because the believers are mentioned before and after it: before it is "li-yudkhila" and after it is ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. The rest read with the tā' as address, and Abu Hatim preferred this.

﴿And honor him﴾: i.e., you magnify him and exalt him; said by al-Hasan and al-Kalbi. Ta'zir means magnifying and esteeming. Qatadah said: you help him and protect him from (harm). Alā bakarat Mayy bi-ghayri safāhatin... tuʿātibu wa-l-mawdūdu yanfaʿuhu al-ʿazr

La-ʿamrī la-anta al-bayt ukrimu ahlahu... wa-ajlisu fī afyā'ihi bi-l-aṣāʾil

(The verse is by Abu Dhu'ayb.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you﴾ at al-Hudaybiyah, O Muhammad. "They are only pledging allegiance to Allah." He made clear that their pledge to His Prophet ﷺ is in fact a pledge to Allah, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾[[Verse 80 of Surah al-Nisa'.]] [al-Nisa': 80]. This pledge is the Pledge of Ridwan (the Pledge of Good Pleasure), as its explanation will come in this surah, God willing, exalted is He. "The hand of Allah is over their hands." It was said: His hand in reward is over their hands in fulfilment (of the pledge), and His hand in bestowing favour upon them through guidance is over their hands in obedience. Al-Kalbi said: its meaning is that Allah's blessing upon them is greater than what they did in pledging allegiance. Ibn Kaysan said: the might of Allah and His support are over their might and their support. "So whoever breaks (his oath)," after the pledge. "Then he breaks it only to his own detriment," i.e., the harm of breaking the pledge returns upon him, because he has deprived himself of reward and bound himself to punishment. "And whoever fulfils what he has covenanted with Allah," it was said: concerning the pledge; and it was said: concerning his faith. "Then We will give him a great reward," meaning in Paradise.

Hafs and al-Zuhri read "ʿalayhu" with a dammah on the ha'. The rest read it with a kasrah. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "fa-sanu'tihi" with the nun. This was preferred by al-Farra' and Abu Mu'adh. The rest read it with the ya'. This is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim, because the name of Allah is closer to it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who lagged behind among the Bedouins will say to you﴾. Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the Bedouins of Ghifar, Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Aslam, Ashja' and al-Dil, and they are the Bedouins who were around Madinah. They lagged behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he intended to travel to Makkah in the year of the Conquest, after he had called them to go out with him, fearing Quraysh. He had entered the state of ihram for 'umrah and had brought the sacrificial animals with him, so that the people would know that he did not intend war. But they were sluggish toward him and made excuses of being busy, so this was revealed. He said "those who lagged behind" because Allah left them behind from accompanying His Prophet. And al-Mukhallaf means the one who is left behind. This has already been discussed in "Bara'ah" (see vol. 8, p. 216). ﴿Our wealth and our families have kept us busy﴾, meaning: there is no one among us to attend to them both. ﴿So ask forgiveness for us﴾: they came seeking forgiveness while their belief was contrary to their outward speech, so Allah exposed them with His saying: ﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾, and this is pure hypocrisy. ﴿Say: Who then can avail you anything against Allah if He intends you harm?﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "ḍurran" with a ḍammah on the ḍad here only, meaning a matter that harms you. Ibn 'Abbas said: defeat.

The rest read it with a fathah, and it is the verbal noun of "darartuhu darran" (I harmed him). With a ḍammah it is a noun for what a person suffers of emaciation and bad condition. The verbal noun may denote a single instance and more. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, saying: because it is paired with benefit (nafʿ), which is the opposite of harm (ḍarr). It was also said: both are two dialectal forms with the same meaning, like al-faqr and al-fuqr, and al-ḍaʿf and al-ḍuʿf. ﴿Or if He intends you benefit﴾, meaning victory and booty. This is a refutation of them when they thought that lagging behind the Messenger would ward off harm from them and hasten benefit for them.

"And that you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families. ﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families ever.﴾" That is because they said: Muhammad and his companions are a morsel (ʾakalat raʾs [[That is, a few people whom one head would satisfy.]]) who will not return. ﴿And that was made attractive﴾, i.e., hypocrisy, ﴿in your hearts﴾. This adornment is from Satan, or Allah creates it in their hearts. ﴿And you thought an evil thought﴾, that Allah would not help His Messenger. ﴿And you were a people ruined (bur)﴾, i.e., perishing; this is said by Mujahid. Qatadah said: corrupt, unfit for any good. Al-Jawhari said: al-bur is the corrupt, perishing man who has no good in him. ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zibaʿra al-Sahmi said:

O Messenger of the King, indeed my tongue
is a stitcher of what I unstitched, when I was bur

A woman is also bur, related by Abu ʿUbayd. And qawm bur means perishing people. Allah says: ﴿And you were a people ruined (qawman burā)﴾, and it is the plural of bāʾir, like ḥāʾil and ḥawl. Fulan bara means he perished, and Allah abarahu means He destroyed him. It has also been said: burā means wicked people; this is said by Ibn Bahr. Hassan ibn Thabit said:

Length (of beard) does not benefit from the foolishness of men, and yet
God guides the path of the bur group

Ay, the perishing.
"And a threat for them, and a clarification that they disbelieved through hypocrisy."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 14:

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wwills, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (48:14)

That is, He is free of need from His servants. He tested them with the obligations (al-taklif) so that He might reward those who believe and punish those who disbelieve and disobey.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 15:

God's words: ﴿Those who were left behind will say, when you set out to take spoils, "Let us follow you."﴾ He means the spoils of Khaybar, because God, mighty and majestic, had promised the people of al-Hudaybiyah the conquest of Khaybar, and that it would belong to them exclusively, whether they were absent or present. None of them was absent from it except Jabir ibn Abd Allah, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave him a share like that of those who were present. Ibn Ishaq said: The one in charge of the division at Khaybar was Jabbar ibn Sakhr al-Ansari of Banu Salamah, and Zayd ibn Thabit of Banu al-Najjar; the two were calculators and dividers.

"Dharuna nattabi'kum" means "leave us": one says "dharhu," meaning "leave him," and "yadharuhu," meaning "he leaves him." Its root is "wadhira yadhiru," on the pattern of "wasi'ahu yasa'uhu." The verbal noun (masdar) has been dropped from use: [[This phrase is from the Asl and the Sihah of al-Jawhari. The wording of al-Lisan: "The Arabs have dropped the masdar and the past tense from 'yadhar,' so it is not said..." etc.]] one does not say "wadharahu" or "wadhir," but rather "taraka-hu" (he left him), and he is "tarik" (one who leaves). Mujahid said: They stayed behind from going out to Makkah. When the Prophet (ﷺ) set out and took a group of them with him, they said: "Leave us, that we may follow you and fight alongside you."

"They want to change the words of God" means they want to alter them. Ibn Zayd said: this refers to His words ﴿So if God brings you back to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, say: You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me﴾ [[Verse 83 of Surah al-Tawbah.]] [al-Tawbah: 83], and so on. Al-Tabari and others rejected this view on the grounds that the expedition of Tabuk took place after the conquest of Khaybar and after the conquest of Makkah. It has also been said: the meaning is that they want to change God's promise made to the people of al-Hudaybiyah, for God had made the spoils of Khaybar a compensation for the conquest of Makkah, since they had returned from al-Hudaybiyah with a truce. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah, and al-Tabari chose it, and it is the view of most of the exegetes.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "kalim" without the alif and with a kasrah on the lam, as the plural of "kalimah," like "salimah" and "salim." The rest read "kalam" as a masdar. Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, on the basis of His words ﴿I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech﴾ [[Verse 144 of Surah al-A'raf.]] [al-A'raf: 144]. "Kalam" is what stands on its own as a complete sentence. Al-Jawhari said: "kalam" is a collective noun applying to the few and the many. "Kalim" cannot be fewer than three words, since it is the plural of "kalimah," like "nabiqah" and "nabiq." This is why Sibawayh said: "This is the chapter on knowing what the kalim (words) of Arabic are," and did not say "kalam," because he meant the three things themselves: the noun, the verb and the particle. So he used a term that only occurs as a plural, and left aside what can apply to both the singular and the plural. The Tamim say "hiya kilmah," with a kasrah on the kaf, and the discussion of this has already passed under "Bara'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 149.]].

"Thus God has said, before this" means: before our return from al-Hudaybiyah, that the spoils of Khaybar belong exclusively to those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah. "Then they will say, 'No, you envy us'" meaning that we should gain some of the spoils with you. It is also said that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If you go out, I will not stop you, except that you have no share." They said: "This is envy." The Muslims said: God told us at al-Hudaybiyah what they would say, and that is His words "Then they will say, 'No, you envy us.'" Then God said: "Rather, they did not understand except a little," meaning they only know the affairs of this world. It has also been said: they understand little of the affairs of religion, namely abandoning fighting.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 16:

There are four issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to the bedouins who were left behind﴾, i.e., say to those who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyah. "You will be called to a people of great might." Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, Ibn Abi Layla and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: they are Persia (Fars). Ka'b, al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla said: the Byzantines (al-Rum). And it is also reported from al-Hasan: Persia and the Byzantines. Ibn Jubayr said: Hawazin and Thaqif. 'Ikrimah said: Hawazin. Qatadah said: Hawazin and Ghatafan on the day of Hunayn. al-Zuhri and Muqatil said: Banu Hanifah, the people of al-Yamamah, the companions of Musaylimah. Rafi' ibn Khadij said: "By Allah, we used to recite this verse in the past, 'You will be called to a people of great might,' and we did not know who they were until Abu Bakr called us to fight Banu Hanifah, and then we knew that they were them." Abu Hurayrah said: "This verse has not yet come." But the apparent meaning of the verse refutes him.

The second: In this verse there is evidence for the validity of the imamate of Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, because Abu Bakr called them to fight Banu Hanifah, and 'Umar called them to fight Persia and the Byzantines. As for the statement of 'Ikrimah and Qatadah that this refers to Hawazin and Ghatafan on the day of Hunayn, it is not so, because it is impossible that the one calling them was the Messenger, peace be upon him, since he said: "You will never go out with me, nor will you fight an enemy with me" [[Qur'an 9:83.]], which shows that the one meant by the caller is other than the Prophet ﷺ. And it is known that after the Prophet ﷺ, none called these people except Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. al-Zamakhshari said: If that is authentically reported from Qatadah, then the meaning is: "You will never go out with me ever, as long as you remain in your present state of sickness of the hearts and confusion regarding the religion."

Or, according to the saying of Mujahid, the promise was that they would not follow the Messenger of Allah ﷺ except as volunteers, having no share in the booty. And Allah knows best [[Addition from manuscripts B, Z, K, N.]].

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will fight them or they will submit﴾. This is the ruling for those from whom the jizyah is not taken. It is joined to "you will fight them," meaning one of two matters must occur: either fighting or Islam, with no third alternative between them. In the reading of Ubayy, "or they will submit" [أو يسلموا] carries the meaning of "until they submit," as you say: "Eat, or you will be satisfied," meaning "until you are satisfied." He said:

"I said to him: do not let your eye weep, for we only seek a kingdom, or we die and are excused."

[[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays.]]

al-Zajjaj said: He said "or they will submit" because the meaning is: "or they submit without fighting." And this applies to fighting the polytheists, not to the People of the Book.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you obey, Allah will give you a good reward﴾, namely spoils and victory in this world, and Paradise in the Hereafter. "But if you turn away as you turned away before" refers to the year of al-Hudaybiyah. "He will punish you with a painful punishment," which is the punishment of the Fire.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When the verse "And if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment" was revealed, the people afflicted with disabilities said: "What about us, O Messenger of Allah?" Then the verse was revealed: "There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick," meaning there is no sin upon them for staying behind from jihad because of their blindness, their disability, and their weakness. The discussion of this has already passed, explained, in Bara'a (Surat al-Tawba) and elsewhere [[see vol. 8, p. 226, and vol. 12, p. 312]]. Al-ʿaraj (lameness) is a affliction affecting one leg; and if that has an effect, then the impairment of both legs is more deserving of having an effect.

Muqatil said: They are the people with disabilities who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyya, and He excused them; that is, whoever among them wishes to march with you to Khaybar, let him do so. "And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger" in what He commands him. "He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow." Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read "nudkhiluhu" with the nun, in the plural of majesty. The rest read it with the ya'. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, because the name of Allah comes first. "And whoever turns away, He will punish him with a painful punishment."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 48, verses 18–19:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾. This is the **Pledge of al-Ridwan** (the Pledge of Divine Pleasure), and it took place at **al-Hudaybiyya**. Here is a brief account of the event of al-Hudaybiyya. The Prophet ﷺ settled after his return from the **Battle of Bani al-Mustaliq** in Shawwal, then set out in Dhu al-Qa'da as a pilgrim for *'umra* (the lesser pilgrimage). He summoned the Bedouin Arabs who surrounded Madina, but most of them lagged behind. The Prophet ﷺ set out with those who were with him of the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and those Arabs who followed him. All of them were about one thousand four hundred. It was also said: one thousand five hundred. Other figures were also mentioned, as will come. He took the sacrificial animals with him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered the state of *ihram* so that people would know that he had not set out for war. When the Quraysh learned of his departure, their people went out to prevent the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from reaching the Sacred Mosque and entering Makka, and [they resolved that] if he fought them, they would fight him in defence of that. They sent Khalid ibn al-Walid ahead with cavalry to **Kura' al-Ghamim** [[Lasmam is a place between Makka and Madina.]]. The news of this reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was at **'Usfan** [['Usfan (with the first letter vowelled with a *damma* and the second letter sukun): a station on the road between al-Juhfa and Makka. It was also said: two stages from Makka on the road to Madina.

(*Mu'jam al-Buldan*).]] The one who informed him was Bishr ibn Sufyan al-Ka'bi. He took a route by which he went out behind them, and he reached al-Hudaybiyya from the lower part of Makka. His guide among them was a man from Aslam. When this reached the cavalry of Quraysh that were with Khalid, they rode to Quraysh to inform them of it. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reached al-Hudaybiyya [[What is between the two brackets is missing from manuscript K.]] his camel knelt down, and the people said: "She has stopped! She has stopped!" [[*Khalat al-naqa*: the she-camel became sullen and knelt down without any cause.]] The Prophet ﷺ said: "She has not stopped, and that is not her habit. Rather, the one who withheld her is the One who withheld the Elephant from Makka. Quraysh will not ask me today for any arrangement in which they seek the maintenance of kinship ties except that I will give it to them." [Then the Prophet ﷺ dismounted there. It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, there is no water in this valley!" So peace and blessings be upon him drew an arrow from his quiver and gave it to one of his companions, and he descended into one of those wells and planted it in its bottom, and the water gushed forth abundantly]

until it sufficed the whole army. It was also said that the one who descended into the well with the arrow was Najiya ibn Jundub ibn 'Umayr al-Aslami, who was the driver of the Prophet's ﷺ sacrificial camels on that day. It was also said that al-Bara' ibn 'Azib descended into the well with the arrow. Then envoys went back and forth between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the negotiation and disputing dragged on until Suhayl ibn 'Amr al-'Amiri came to him, and he made an agreement with him that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would return that year. The following year, he would come for *'umra* and he and his companions would enter Makka without weapons, except swords in their sheaths. He would stay there three days and then leave. There would be a truce between him and them for ten years, during which people could mix and be safe from one another. It was also agreed that whoever came from the disbelievers to the Muslims as a Muslim, man or woman, would be returned to the disbelievers, and whoever came from the Muslims to the disbelievers as an apostate would not be returned to the Muslims. This was very grievous for the Muslims, to the point that some of them spoke about it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, knowing what Allah had taught him, that He would make a way out for the Muslims, said to his companions: [[Be patient, for Allah will make this truce a means to the manifestation of His religion.]] The people were reassured by his words after their unease, but Suhayl ibn 'Amr refused to write at the head of the treaty document: "From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah." They said to him: "Even if we affirmed that to you, it would not stop us from opposing what you intend! You must write: 'In your name, O Allah.'" He said to 'Ali, who was writing the treaty document: [[Erase it, O 'Ali, and write: 'In your name, O Allah.']] But 'Ali refused to erase with his own hand "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: [[Show it to me.]] So he pointed to it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ erased it with his own hand, and ordered him to write [[From Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah.]]. On that day Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl came with the marks of the treaty document, dragging his feet in his shackles, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned him to his father. This was very grievous to the Muslims, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed them and informed Abu Jandal [[that Allah would make for him a relief and a way out.]]. Before the treaty, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had sent 'Uthman ibn 'Affan to Makka as an envoy. Then news reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that the people of Makka had killed him. At that point the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called for a pledge of allegiance from them to fight and wage war against the people of Makka. It is related that he took their pledge to die [in battle]. It is also related that he took their pledge not to flee. This is the Pledge of al-Ridwan under the tree, concerning which Allah the Exalted informed that He was pleased with those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ beneath it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ also informed that they would not enter the Fire. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ struck his right hand upon his left for 'Uthman, so he is like one who witnessed it. Waki' reported from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from al-Sha'bi, who said: "The first to pledge allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of al-Hudaybiyya was Abu Sufyan al-Asadi." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, who said: "On the day of al-Hudaybiyya we were one thousand four hundred. We pledged allegiance to him while 'Umar was holding his hand beneath the tree, and it was a *samura* tree [[*al-Samura*: the acacia tree.]]." And he said: "We pledged allegiance to him that we would not flee, and we did not pledge allegiance to him for death." **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 20:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God promised you many spoils that you will take﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: these are the spoils that will come until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Zayd said: they are the spoils of Khaybar. "So He hastened this for you" means Khaybar, as Mujahid said. Ibn 'Abbas said: He hastened for you the treaty of Hudaybiyyah. "And restrained the hands of the people from you" means the people of Makkah, whom He restrained from you through the treaty. Qatadah said: He restrained the hands of the Jews from Madinah after the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to Hudaybiyyah and Khaybar. This is the view chosen by al-Tabari, because the restraining of the hands of the polytheists at Hudaybiyyah is mentioned in His saying: ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you﴾[[The 24th verse of this surah.]] [al-Fath: 24].

Ibn 'Abbas also said: "And restrained the hands of the people from you" means 'Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari, 'Awf ibn Malik al-Nadri and those who were with them, when they came to support the people of Khaybar while the Prophet (ﷺ) was besieging them. So God, mighty and majestic, cast terror into their hearts and restrained them from the Muslims. "And that it might be a sign for the believers" means that their defeat and your safety would be a sign for the believers, so that they would know that God protects them both when they are present and when they are absent. It was also said: that is, and that the restraining of their hands from you would be a sign for the believers. And it was said: that is, and that this which He hastened for you would be a sign for the believers of your truthfulness, in that you promised them that they would obtain it.

The wāw in "wa-li-takūna" (وَلِتَكُونَ) is superfluous (muqhamah) according to the Kufans (the grammarians of Kufa). The Basrans (the grammarians of Basra) said it is conjunctive (ʿāṭifah), coordinating with an implied element, meaning: "And He restrained the hands of the people from you so that you would give thanks to Him, and so that it would be a sign for the believers." ﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾ means: He will increase you in guidance, or make you firm in guidance.

"Wa-ukhrā" (and another [gain]): "ukhrā" is coordinated with "hādhihi," meaning: He hastened for you these spoils and other spoils. "Lam taqdirū ʿalayhā qad aḥāṭa Allāh bihā" (which you were not able to obtain, but Allah has encompassed them). Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the conquests that were opened to the Muslims, such as the lands of Persia and Byzantium, and all that the Muslims conquered. This is also the view of al-Ḥasan, Muqātil and Ibn Abī Layla. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbās also, and from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Isḥāq: they are Khaybar, which Allah promised His Prophet before he conquered it, and they had not been hoping for it until Allah informed them of it. And it is related from al-Ḥasan also, and Qatādah: it is the conquest of Makkah. ʿIkrimah said: Ḥunayn, because He said "lam taqdirū ʿalayhā." This indicates an earlier attempt at it and the loss of attaining the desired thing at the time, as was the case in Makkah, as al-Qushayrī said. Mujāhid said: they are whatever will occur until the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of "qad aḥāṭa Allāh bihā" is that He prepared them for you; they are like a thing that has been encircled on all sides, so it is confined and cannot escape. So even if you were not able to obtain them at present, they are held in reserve for you and will not escape you. It was also said: "aḥāṭa Allāh bihā" means He knew that they would be yours, as He said: "wa-anna Allāh qad aḥāṭa bi-kulli shayʾin ʿilmā" [[Verse 12 of Surah al-Talaq.]] [al-Talaq: 12]. And it was said: Allah preserved them for you, so that their conquest would be for you. "Wa-kāna Allāh ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīran."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 22–23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if those who disbelieve had fought against you, they would have turned their backs﴾. Qatadah said: It refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh at al-Hudaybiyah. It was also said: "And if they had fought against you" refers to Ghatafan, Asad, and those who intended to aid the people of Khaybar; the outcome would have been against them. ﴿Then they would not find any ally or helper﴾. ﴿The way of Allah which has already occurred before, and you will not find in the way of Allah any change﴾. That is: the custom and practice of Allah in the past, which is the granting of victory to His allies over His enemies. Al-sunnah (the way, course of conduct) means the path and the conduct. A poet said:

So do not be distressed by a conduct you yourself have followed, for the first to be content with a way is the one who follows it.
