His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah﴾. It refers to al-Hudaybiyah. "After He had given you victory over them." Yazid ibn Harun narrated, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah informed us, from Thabit, from Anas, that eighty men of the people of Makkah descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ) from the mountain of al-Tan'im [[al-Tan'im: a place in Makkah in the area outside the sacred precinct, between Makkah and Sarif.]], armed, intending to catch the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions off guard [[al-ghirrah (with a kasra): heedlessness, i.e., they intended to find the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions unprepared.]]. We seized them alive [[The narration of Muslim reads: "He seized them alive (salman) and spared them." Regarding the word "salman," Ibn al-Athir said: "It is narrated with a kasra or a fatha on the sin, and both are dialectal forms meaning peace/settlement, and this is what is meant in the hadith, as explained by al-Humaydi in his *Gharib*. Al-Khattabi said it is *al-silm* with a fatha on the sin and lam, meaning surrender and submission... and this is closer to the matter, for they were not taken under a treaty, but were seized by force and surrendered themselves out of helplessness..."]] alive, and we spared them. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: "And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah, after He had given you victory over them."

Abdullah ibn Mughaffal al-Muzani said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) at al-Hudaybiyah, under the tree that Allah mentioned in the Qur'an. While we were like that, thirty young men armed with weapons came out upon us and charged at our faces. The Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against them, and Allah seized their sight. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: [Have you come under the covenant of anyone, or has anyone granted you safe conduct?] They said: "No, by Allah." So he released them. Then Allah revealed: "And it is He who restrained their hands from you," to the end of the verse.

Ibn Hisham narrated from Waki': Some seventy or eighty men of the Quraysh had come to strike the Muslims and seize an opportunity against them at their outskirts. The Muslims became aware of them and took them as captives. This happened while the envoys were going back and forth between them regarding the peace. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) released them. They are the ones called *al-'Utaqa'* (the freed ones), and among them were Mu'awiyah and his father.

Mujahid said: The Prophet (ﷺ) came in the state of ihram for 'umrah, when his Companions seized some people from the sacred precinct who were heedless, and the Prophet (ﷺ) released them. That is the "victory" in the valley of Makkah.

Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that a man from among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), called Zunaym, looked out over the ridge of al-Hudaybiyah, and the polytheists shot him with an arrow and killed him. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent a cavalry, and they brought twelve horsemen from the disbelievers. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: [Do you have a covenant with me?] They said: "No." So he released them, and then this was revealed.

Ibn Abza and al-Kalbi said: They were the people of al-Hudaybiyah. Allah restrained their hands from the Muslims until the peace was concluded, although they had come out in full force intending to attack the Muslims, and He restrained the hands of the Muslims from them.

It has already been mentioned that Khalid ibn al-Walid was among the cavalry of the polytheists.

Al-Qushayri said: This is a narration, but the correct view is that he was with the Prophet (ﷺ) at that time. [[A marginal note found in the handwriting of the copyist in manuscript K reads: Someone commented on this statement and said: This is false; Khalid ibn al-Walid embraced Islam long after al-Hudaybiyah. He said: Even if Ibn Abd al-Barr mentioned that he was over the cavalry of the Muslims at al-Hudaybiyah, that is an error. Some have said: Far be it from Ibn Abd al-Barr to hold such a view, for he had mentioned two pages earlier that Khalid was over the cavalry of the polytheists on that day, and this is a known matter. But al-Qushayri is not the source of this knowledge, and the author (al-Qurtubi) transmits what he found. Khalid embraced Islam six months after al-Hudaybiyah.]]

Salamah ibn al-Akwa' said: They were discussing the matter of the peace when Abu Sufyan approached, and the valley was moving with men and weapons. He said: I brought six of the polytheists, driving them along, armed, unable to bring any benefit or harm to themselves, and I brought them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Umar had said on the road: "O Messenger of Allah, are we going to a people at war with us while we have no weapons or horses?" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to Madinah from the road, and they brought him every weapon and horse that was there. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed that Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl had come out against you with five hundred horsemen. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Khalid ibn al-Walid: [This is your cousin; he has come to you with five hundred.] Khalid said: "I am the Sword of Allah and the Sword of His Messenger." It was on that day that he was named "the Sword of Allah." He went out with horsemen, defeated the disbelievers, and drove them back to the orchards of Makkah. This narration is more authentic. There was fighting between them with stones, and it was said with arrows and the bowstring [[*al-zufr* (with a damma): the end of the bow.]].

It was also said: By the restraint of hands is meant that the treaty stipulated that whoever came to us from them would be returned to them. Some men from Makkah who had embraced Islam went out, fearing the Messenger (peace be upon him) would return them to the polytheists, and they joined the coast, among them Abu Basir. They began raiding the disbelievers and seizing their caravans, until the leading men of the Quraysh came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Take them to yourself, so that we may be secure." He did so.

It was also said: Ghatafan and Asad intended to prevent the Muslims from the Jews of Khaybar, because they were their allies, but Allah restrained them from that, and this is the restraint of hands.

Regarding "in the valley of Makkah," there are two views: the first is that it means Makkah itself; the second is al-Hudaybiyah, because part of it is attached to the sacred precinct.

Al-Mawardi said: As for His saying "after He had given you victory over them," it refers to the conquest of Makkah. This verse was revealed after the conquest of Makkah, and it indicates that Makkah was conquered by treaty, due to His saying, mighty and majestic is He: "He restrained their hands from you and your hands from them."

I say: The correct view is that this verse was revealed at al-Hudaybiyah before the conquest of Makkah, as we have already mentioned from the people of interpretation among the Companions and the Successors.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated: Abd ibn Humayd told us, saying: Sulayman ibn Harb told me, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah told us, from Thabit, from Anas: that eighty men descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions from the mountain of al-Tan'im at the time of the dawn prayer, intending to kill him. They were seized, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) freed them. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: "And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them," to the end of the verse.

Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a hadith that is *hasan sahih*, and it has already been mentioned.

As for the conquest of Makkah, the reports indicate that it was conquered by force (*'anwatan*), and the discussion of this has already passed in *al-Hajj* [[See vol. 12, p. 33.]] and elsewhere.

﴿And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 25 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and barred the sacrificial animals from reaching their place of sacrifice.﴾ There are three issues.

The first issue concerns His saying ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved﴾, meaning the Quraysh, who prevented you from entering the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, when the Prophet ﷺ and his companions had entered the state of ihram for the 'umrah. They also prevented the sacrificial animals and held them back from reaching their place of sacrifice. They did not believe in this prohibition, but arrogance drove them and the zeal of the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) called them to do what they did not believe to be religion. So Allah rebuked them for this and threatened them over it, and He brought comfort to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ through His explanation and His promise.

The second issue concerns His saying ﴿and the sacrificial animals held back﴾, meaning detained. It was also said: stopped. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: gathered. Al-Jawhari said: 'akafahu means he detained him and stopped him, and he says ya'kifuhu and ya'kufuhu, 'akfan. From this is His saying ﴿and the sacrificial animals held back﴾. It is said: "What has held you back from such-and-such?" From this also comes i'tikaf in the mosque, which is confinement (ihtibas). His saying ﴿reaching their place of sacrifice﴾ means the place where they are slaughtered (mankhar), as al-Farra' said. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Haram (the sacred precinct). Likewise Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the place of sacrifice for the one prevented (al-muhsar) is the Haram.

The word al-mahill (with a kasra on the ha') means the end point of a thing. With a fatha (mahall) it means the place where people alight. The sacrificial animals were seventy camels, but Allah, by His grace, made that place their place of sacrifice. The scholars have differed on this, as was explained earlier in al-Baqarah at His saying ﴿But if you are prevented﴾ [ref. vol. 2, p. 371, second edition]. The correct view is what we have mentioned.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "We sacrificed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, a camel for seven and a cow for seven." He also said: "We shared with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the hajj and the 'umrah, each seven in one camel." A man said to Jabir: "Can one share in a camel the same way one shares in a slaughtered beast?" He said: "It is none other than one of the badanah (camels)." Jabir was present at al-Hudaybiyah and said: "On that day we sacrificed seventy camels, sharing, each seven in one camel."

In al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as those performing 'umrah, but the disbelievers of Quraysh blocked us from the House. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sacrificed a camel and shaved his head." It was said: the one who shaved his head that day was Khirash ibn Umayyah ibn Abi al-'Is al-Khuza'i. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded the Muslims to sacrifice and exit the state of ihram, but they hesitated, and this hesitation angered the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Umm Salamah said to him: "If you sacrifice, they will sacrifice." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sacrificed his offering, and they sacrificed by his sacrifice. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ shaved his head and prayed for those who shaved three times and for those who trimmed once. He saw Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah with lice falling on his face, and said: [Do your vermin trouble you?] He said: "Yes." So he ordered him to shave, and that was at al-Hudaybiyah. It was narrated by al-Bukhari and al-Daraqutni. This has passed in al-Baqarah [ref. vol. 2, p. 383, second edition].

The third issue concerns His saying ﴿and the sacrificial animals﴾. Al-hadi and al-hady are two dialectal forms. It was read as "until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of sacrifice" (hatta yablugha al-hadyu mahallahu), with and without shaddah. The singular is hadiyyah. This has also passed in al-Baqarah [vol. 2, p. 378]. It is coordinated with the kaf and mim in "barred you" (sadduukum). "MaAkufan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal). The position of "an" in His saying ﴿reaching its place of sacrifice﴾ is accusative by supposition of its being governed by "barred you", meaning: they barred you and barred the sacrificial animals from reaching it. It may also be a causative object, as if He said: "and they barred the sacrificial animals out of dislike that they reach their place of sacrifice." Abu 'Ali said: It is not valid to attach it to "detained", because we do not know of 'akafa being used transitively. The occurrence of ma'kufan in the verse may be understood by sense, as if, since it was a detention, the meaning was taken to be that. Just as ar-rafath was taken in the sense of "going into", and so was followed by ila. If it is taken that way, its position would be accusative according to Sibawayh's analysis, and genitive according to al-Khalil's analysis. Or it may be a causative object, as if He said: detained out of dislike that it reach its place of sacrifice. It is also permissible to posit a preposition (jarr) on "an", because "'an" has already occurred, so it is as if He said: "they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and barred the sacrificial animals from reaching their place of sacrifice." A parallel is what Sibawayh related from Yunus: "I passed by a man, both (in) Zayd and (in) 'Amr," where the preposition is elided because it was mentioned earlier.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had there not been believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby incur blame from them without knowledge.﴾ In this there are three issues.

The first issue concerns His saying ﴿Had there not been believing men and believing women﴾, meaning the weak believers among the disbelievers in Makkah, such as Salamah ibn Hisham, 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl, and their like. ﴿whom you did not know﴾ means whom you did not recognize. It was also said: you did not know that they were believers. ﴿that you might trample them﴾ means by killing and striking them. It is said: "wataat al-qawm," meaning I struck the people. The "an" may be in the nominative as an apposition to "men" and "women", as if He said: "Had it not been your trampling of believing men and believing women." It may also be accusative as an apposition to the ha' and mim in "you did not know them", so that the meaning is: "you did not know their trampling." In both cases it is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition). "You did not know them" is a description of "men" and "women". The answer to "Had there not been" is omitted, and the sense is: "Had it been that you would trample believing men and believing women whom you did not know, Allah would have permitted you to enter Makkah and given you power over them. But We protected those in it who were concealing their faith out of fear." Al-Dahhak said: "Had there not been those in the loins of the disbelievers and the wombs of their women of believing men and believing women, you did not know that you would trample their fathers, and their sons would perish."

The second issue concerns His saying ﴿and thereby incur blame from them﴾. Al-ma'arrah means shame, and it is a mafa'alah from al-'urr, which is scabies. That is, the polytheists would say: "They have killed the people of their own religion." It was also said: the meaning is that the killing would bring upon you what binds you to expiation for accidental killing, because Allah the Exalted only obligated the expiation, not the blood-money, upon the killer of a believer in the land of war, if he had not emigrated from it and his faith was not known, according to His saying: ﴿If he is from a people hostile to you and he is a believer, then the freeing of a believing slave﴾ [al-Nisa': 92]. This was said by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and others. The matter has been discussed earlier in al-Nisa' [ref. vol. 5, p. 323]. Ibn Zayd said: "ma'arrah" means sin. Al-Jawhari and Ibn Ishaq said: the burden of blood-money. Qutrub said: hardship. It was also said: grief.

The third issue concerns His saying ﴿without knowledge﴾. It is a commendation of the Companions and a report of their noble qualities of chastity from disobedience and restraint from transgression, so that even if they had struck any of them, it would have been without intent. This is like what the ant said about the soldiers of Sulayman, peace be upon him, in her saying: ﴿Let not Sulayman and his soldiers crush you while they do not perceive﴾ [al-Naml: 18].

I need to be careful here about one point. The passage contains a hadith attributed to ʿAlī (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) about the Prophet (ﷺ), and the text itself is a faithful transcript of al-Qurtubi's commentary, so I will translate it as it stands.

**Verse 25:** ﴿That He may admit into His mercy whom He wills. Had they been separated⁠—﴾ There are four issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That He may admit into His mercy whom He wills⁠﴾. The lām in "li-yudkhila" (that He may admit) is connected to an omitted element, meaning: had you killed them, Allah would have admitted them into His mercy. It is also permissible for it to be connected to "al-īmān" (faith). It should not be restricted to male believers without female believers, nor to female believers without male believers, because all of them enter into the mercy. It has also been said: the meaning is that Allah did not permit you to fight the polytheists so that those from the people of Makkah whom He had decreed to become Muslim would become Muslim after the truce. Indeed, many of them did become Muslim, their Islam was good, and they entered into His mercy, that is, His Paradise.

**The second issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had they been separated⁠﴾, that is, had they been distinguished (tamayyazū). This was said by al-Qutaybī. It has also been said: had they been dispersed; this was said by al-Kalbī. It has also been said: had the believers departed from among the disbelievers, the disbelievers would have been punished by the sword; this was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. But Allah repels punishment from the disbelievers through the believers.

ʿAlī (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this verse, "Had they been separated, We would have punished those who disbelieved," and he said: [They are the polytheists among the forefathers of the Prophet of Allah and those after them. In their time, there were believing people in their loins. So had the believers been separated from the loins of the disbelievers, Allah, Exalted is He, would have punished the disbelievers with a painful punishment.]

**The third issue:** This verse is evidence for taking the disbeliever's presence into account in respect of the sanctity of the believer, since harming the disbeliever cannot be done without harming the believer. Abū Zayd said: I said to Ibn al-Qāsim: What do you think if a group of polytheists is in one of their fortresses, and the people of Islam besiege them while among them are Muslims taken captive in their hands—will this fortress be burned or not? He said: I heard Mālik and Sayl concerning a group of polytheists in their ships: shall we shoot fire at their ships while the captives are with them in their ships? He said: Mālik said: I do not see that, because of His saying, Exalted is He, to the people of Makkah: "Had they been separated, We would have punished those of them who disbelieved with a painful punishment." Likewise, if a disbeliever shields himself with a Muslim, it is not permissible to shoot him. If someone does so and destroys any Muslim, then he owes the blood-money (diyah) and expiation (kaffārah). If they did not know, there is neither blood-money nor expiation, because when they know, they may not shoot; if they do so, they become killers by mistake, and the blood-money is upon their ʿawāqil (the paternal relatives who bear the blood-money). If they did not know, they may shoot. When the act is permitted to them, no liability for it may remain upon them.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "A group has said its meaning is: had they been separated from the bellies of women and the loins of men. This is weak, because whoever is in the loins or in the belly is not trodden upon and no harm reaches him from it. Yet He, glorified is He, has stated clearly, saying: 'And had there not been believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them.' That does not apply to those in the belly of a woman or the loins of men, but applies to people like al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd, Salamah ibn Hishām, ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah, and Abū Jandal ibn Suhayl. Likewise Mālik said: We besieged the city of the Romans, and water was cut off from them, so they would lower the captives to draw water for them, and no one could shoot them with arrows, so water reached them without our choice. Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions and al-Thawrī permitted shooting into the fortresses of the polytheists even if there were Muslim captives among them and their children. If a disbeliever shields himself with a Muslim child, the polytheist is shot, and if any Muslim is struck, there is no blood-money in it and no expiation. Al-Thawrī said: in it there is expiation but no blood-money. Al-Shāfiʿī agreed with our view. This is evident, for reaching a permitted end through a forbidden means is not allowed, especially with the soul of a Muslim. So there is no opinion except what Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, said. And Allah knows best."

I say: It may be permissible to kill the shield, and there will be no disagreement on it, if Allah wills, when the benefit is necessary, total, and certain. Its being necessary means that reaching the disbelievers is not possible except by killing the shield. Its being total means that it cuts off for the entire community, so that the benefit of killing the shield reaches all the Muslims; if it is not done, the disbelievers will kill the shield and seize the entire community. Its being certain means that this benefit is definitely obtained from killing the shield. Our scholars said: this benefit, with these conditions, should not be disputed regarding its consideration, because the premise is that the shield will certainly be killed: either by the enemy's hands, and then the great harm occurs, which is the enemy's domination over all the Muslims; or by the Muslims' hands, and then the enemy perishes and all the Muslims are saved. No sensible person can say that the shield must not be killed in this case in any way, for that would entail the loss of the shield, Islam and the Muslims. But since this benefit is not free of harm, the soul of whoever has not considered it carefully recoils from it, for that harm, relative to what is gained from it, is nothing or like nothing. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** The common reading is "law tazayyalū" (had they been separated), except that Abū Ḥaywah read "tazāyalū," which in meaning is like "tazayyalū." Al-tazayyul means separation. "Tazayyalū" is tafaʿʿalū, from zil(tu). It has also been said it is tafayʿalū. "La-ʿaḏḏabnā alladhīna kafarū" (We would have punished those who disbelieved). It has been said: the lām is the answer to two statements: one of them, "law-lā rijālun" (had there not been men), and the second, "law tazayyalū" (had they been separated). It has also been said the answer to "law-lā" is omitted, and this has already been mentioned. "Law tazayyalū" is the beginning of a new statement.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 26:

The element governing "idh" (when) is His words, exalted is He: ﴿la-adhdhabnā﴾ (surely We would have punished), meaning: surely We would have punished them when they made this (the zealotry). Or it is a hidden verb whose estimate is "and remember" (udhkurū).

"Al-ḥamiyyah" (zealotry) is of the form fa'īlah, and it means al-anafah (disdain, self-respect that refuses). It is said: "ḥamītu ʿan kadhā ḥamiyyatan" (with shaddah) and "maḥmiyyatan" when you disdain it and shame and disdain enter you about doing it. From this is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

Indeed I am of them, and my honour is their honour,
Like the one with the nose who protects his nose from being cut off.

That is, he prevents (it). Al-Zuhri said: "Their zealotry was their disdain from acknowledging the Prophet ﷺ as a messenger, and from opening with "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and their preventing him from entering Makkah. The one who refused to write "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" and "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah" was Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, as has preceded." Ibn Bahr said: "Their zealotry was their partisanship for their gods which they worshipped besides Allah, exalted is He, and their disdain at worshipping anything other than them."

It was also said: "the zealotry of the Jahiliyyah" (ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyyah): they said, "They killed our sons and brothers, then they enter upon us in our homes, and by al-Lat and al-ʿUzza, they shall never enter it."

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility﴾, that is, the calm and dignity (al-ṭuma'nīnah wa al-waqār), ﴿upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾. It was also said: He made them steadfast in contentment and submission, and did not place in their hearts what He placed in the hearts of those people of zealotry.

﴿And He made them adhere to the word of piety﴾. It was said: it is "lā ilāha illā Allāh" (there is no god but Allah). This was narrated with a marfūʿ chain from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb from the Prophet ﷺ. It is also the view of ʿAli, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, Salamah ibn Kuhayl, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Talhah ibn Musarrif, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani said it too, and added "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Also from ʿAli and Ibn ʿUmar: it is "lā ilāha illā Allāh, Allāhu akbar." ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah and Mujahid also said: it is "lā ilāha illā Allāh waḥdahu lā sharīka lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-ḥamd wa huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr." Al-Zuhri said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." He means that the polytheists did not acknowledge this word, so Allah singled out the believers with it. The "word of piety" is that by which one guards against shirk. Also from Mujahid: the "word of piety" is sincerity (al-ikhlas).

﴿And they were more worthy of it and fit for it﴾, that is, more worthy of it than the disbelievers of Makkah, because Allah, exalted is He, chose them for His religion and for the companionship of His Prophet.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾.

Qatadah said: The Messenger of God ﷺ had seen in a dream that he would enter Makkah in this manner. When he made the treaty with the Quraysh at al-Hudaybiyah, the hypocrites doubted, until the Messenger of God ﷺ said that he would enter Makkah. God then revealed, "God has indeed fulfilled His Messenger's vision with truth," informing them that they would enter in a year other than that one, and that the vision of the Prophet ﷺ is true. It is also said that Abu Bakr was the one who said that the dream was not tied to a specific time, and that he would enter. It is narrated that the vision occurred at al-Hudaybiyah, and that the visions of the prophets are true, and that a vision is one of the modes of revelation to the prophets.

"You will surely enter" means: in the coming year, "the Sacred Mosque, if God wills." Ibn Kaysan said: this is a report of what was said to the Prophet ﷺ in his dream. He was addressed in his dream with what is customary, and God informed about His Messenger that he said that. For this reason he made the exception, adhering to the etiquette of God the Exalted, when He said: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [with the qualification], "If Allah wills."﴾ [Al-Kahf: 23–24]. [Verse 23 of Surah al-Kahf.]

It is also said: God addressed the servants with what He loves them to say, as He said, "And never say of anything, 'Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,' except [with the qualification], 'If Allah wills.'" It is also said: He made the exception regarding what He knows, so that people might make the exception regarding what they do not know; this was said by Tha'lab. It is also said: God knew that He would cause some of those who were with him at al-Hudaybiyah to die, so the exception occurred for this meaning; this was said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. It is also said: the exception applies to "secure," and this returns to addressing the servants according to what is customary. It is also said: the meaning of "if God wills" is: if God commands you to enter. It is also said: that is, if God facilitates it. It is also said: "if God wills" means: as God wills. Abu Ubaydah said: "in" here means "since," i.e., since God willed, like His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest, if you are [truly] believers﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 278] [Verse 278 of Surah al-Baqarah], meaning: since you are believers. But this is far-fetched, because "idh" is used for the past tense of the verb, and "idha" for the future, and this entering is in the future. So He promised them entry into the Sacred Mosque and tied it to the condition of God's will. That was the year of al-Hudaybiyah. He informed his companions of this and they rejoiced. Then that was delayed beyond the year for which they had hoped, which grieved them and weighed heavily upon them, and he made peace with them and returned. Then God permitted it in the following year, and God revealed, "God has indeed fulfilled His Messenger's vision with truth." He was told in the dream, "You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills," and in the revelation He related what was said to him in the dream. There is therefore no doubt here, as some have claimed that the exception indicates doubt, while God the Exalted does not doubt, and "you will surely enter" is an affirmation, so how could there be doubt? So "in" means "if" (idha).

"Secure" means: safe from the enemy. "Shaving your heads and cutting short [your hair]": shaving and cutting short are both for men, and for this reason the masculine is given precedence over the feminine. Shaving is more excellent, and women have only cutting short. This matter has been discussed before in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 2, p. 381, second edition.] It is recorded in the Sahih that Mu'awiyah took some of the hair of the Prophet ﷺ at Marwah with a small shears. This was during the 'umrah, not the hajj, because the Prophet ﷺ shaved during his hajj.

"Fearing no one" is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to those shaving and cutting, and the implied meaning is: not fearful. "So He knew what you did not know": that is, He knew the good and benefit in delaying entry, which you did not know. That is because when he ﷺ returned from it, he went from there to Khaybar and conquered it, and returned with the wealth of Khaybar, and took in equipment and strength many times what he had had in that year, and came toward Makkah with preparation, strength and equipment many times that amount. Al-Kalbi said: that is, He knew that entering it would be after a year, and you did not know that. It is also said: He knew that in Makkah there were believing men and believing women whom you did not know.

"So He made, besides that, a near conquest": that is, besides the Prophet's ﷺ vision, the conquest of Khaybar; this was said by Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak. It is also said that it was the conquest of Makkah. Mujahid said: it is the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, and most of the exegetes said so. Al-Zuhri said: No conquest that God made in Islam was greater than the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, because fighting only occurred when people met. When there was a truce, war laid down its burdens, people became secure with one another, they met, and they discussed and debated. No one who was intelligent was addressed about Islam without entering it. Indeed, in those two years, the number who entered Islam was equal to what had entered it before, and more. This is shown by the fact that at al-Hudaybiyah in the sixth year they were 1,400, and after the year of al-Hudaybiyah, in the eighth year, they were 10,000.

**"He it is who sent His Messenger"** (﴿هُوَ الَّذِي أَرْسَلَ رَسُولَهُ﴾): meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). **"with guidance and the religion of truth, so that He may make it prevail over all religion"** (﴿بِالْهُدَىٰ وَدِينِ الْحَقِّ لِيُظْهِرَهُ عَلَى الدِّينِ كُلِّهِ﴾), i.e., He will exalt it above all religions. The word *al-din* (religion) is a noun used in the sense of a verbal noun (*masdar*), and its singular and plural forms are the same.

It has also been said: the meaning is that He will make His Messenger prevail over all religion, that is, over the religion that He legislated, through proof (*hujjah*) and then through the hand and the sword, and that it abrogated (*nasakha*, i.e., *naskh*, abrogation) whatever was other than it. **"And Allah suffices as a witness"** (﴿وَكَفَىٰ بِاللَّهِ شَهِيدًا﴾). The word *shahidan* (شَهِيدًا) is in the accusative as a *tafsir* (an explanatory specification, i.e., a *tamyiz*-like clarification), and the *ba'* (بِ) is superfluous (*za'idah*, additional). The meaning is: Allah suffices as a witness for His Prophet (ﷺ), and His witnessing for him demonstrates the truth of his prophethood through the miracles.

It has also been said: *shahidan* means a witness to what he was sent with, because the disbelievers refused to write: "This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, agreed upon."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 48, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

There are five issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of God﴾. "Muhammad" is the *mubtada'* (subject of the nominal sentence) and "Messenger" is its *khabar* (predicate). It is also said that "Muhammad" is the beginning of the sentence and "Messenger of God" is its *na't* (qualifier). "And those with him" is conjoined to the subject, and the predicate is what follows it. On this reading, one should not pause at "Messenger of God." On the first reading, one pauses at "Messenger of God," because the attributes of the Prophet, peace be upon him, exceed what is ascribed to his companions. So "Muhammad" is the subject and "Messenger of God" the predicate, and "those with him" is a second subject. "Harsh (ashidda') against the disbelievers" is its predicate, and "merciful (ruhama') among themselves" is a second predicate. That the attributes apply to the whole body of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ is the more likely reading.

Ibn Abbas said: the people of Hudaybiyya are "harsh against the disbelievers," meaning severe toward them, like a lion toward its prey. It is also said that "those with him" refers to all believers. "Merciful among themselves" means that they show mercy to one another. It is also said that they are compassionate and affectionate toward one another.

al-Hasan read "harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves" in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative), as if to say: "and those with him, in their harshness against the disbelievers and their mercy toward one another." ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating﴾ is a report of the great number of their prayers. ﴿Seeking bounty from God and His good pleasure﴾ means they seek Paradise and the pleasure of God, exalted is He.

The second concerns God's words: ﴿Their mark is on their faces from the traces of prostration﴾. *Simâ* means "mark," and it has two forms, with the long vowel and with the short one. That is, the signs of night vigil and the marks of wakefulness appear.

In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, he said: Ismail ibn Muhammad al-Talhi narrated to us, he said: Thabit ibn Musa Abu Yazid narrated to us, from Shurayk, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from Jabir, who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever's prayer is abundant at night, his face will be beautiful by day."

Ibn al-Arabi said: some people inserted this into the Prophet's ﷺ hadith by mistake, and there is no mention of the Prophet ﷺ regarding it in any form. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik: "Their mark is on their faces from the traces of prostration" refers to what is related to their foreheads from the ground during prostration. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said this.

In the authentic hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: he led the prayer on the morning of the twenty-first of Ramadan, when the mosque was dripping [[i.e., its roof was leaking]], and it had a palm-frond roof. When the Prophet ﷺ finished his prayer, there were traces of water and mud on his forehead and the tip of his nose.

al-Hasan said: it is a whiteness that appears on the face on the Day of Resurrection. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said this. al-Awfi narrated it from Ibn Abbas, and al-Zuhri said it.

In the Sahih, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, and in it: "When God has finished judging among His servants and wishes to bring out by His mercy whom He wills from the people of the Fire, He commands the angels to bring out of the Fire whoever did not associate anything with God, whom God wills to show mercy, those who say 'There is no god but God.' They will recognize them in the Fire by the traces of prostration. The Fire will consume the son of Adam except the traces of prostration; God has forbidden the Fire to consume the traces of prostration."

Shahr ibn Hawshab said: the place of prostration on their faces will be like the moon on the night of the full moon.

Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: the *simâ* is in this world, and it is the good bearing (*samt*). Also from Mujahid: it is humility and lowliness. Mansur said: I asked Mujahid about God's words, "Their mark is on their faces," whether it is a mark that appears between a man's eyes. He said: No, sometimes there is between a man's eyes something like the knee of a goat, and he is harder of heart than stones! Rather, it is a light on their faces from humility.

Ibn Juraij said: it is gravity and splendor. Shimr ibn Atiyya said: it is the paleness of the face from standing in prayer at night. al-Hasan said: "When you see them, you think they are sick, and they are not sick." al-Dahhak said: "Surely it is not a wound on their faces, but it is paleness." Sufyan al-Thawri said: they pray at night, and when they awake, that appears on their faces. Its explanation is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Whoever's prayer is abundant at night, his face will be beautiful by day." This has already been discussed just above. Ata al-Khurasani said: everyone who maintains the five daily prayers is included in this verse.

The third concerns God's words: ﴿That is their likeness in the Torah, and their likeness in the Gospel﴾. al-Farra' said: there are two possibilities. If you wish, you may say the meaning is: "That is their likeness in the Torah, and in the Gospel as well, like their likeness in the Qur'an," in which case the pause falls at "the Gospel." If you wish, you may say: the sentence is complete at "That is their likeness in the Torah," and then a new sentence begins: "and their likeness in the Gospel."

Ibn Abbas and others likewise said: these are two likenesses, one in the Torah and the other in the Gospel, and on this view one pauses at "the Torah." Mujahid said: it is one likeness, meaning that this is their description in both the Torah and the Gospel, so on this view one does not pause at "the Torah" but pauses at "the Gospel."

The sentence begins with "like a seed that sends out its shoot" in the sense of "they are like a seed." *Shatʾahu* means its offshoots and its young shoots, as said by Ibn Zayd and others. Muqatil said: it is one plant, and when what comes after it emerges, it has produced shoots.

al-Jawhari said: *shatʾ* of a crop or plant is its offshoots, and the plural is *ashtâʾ*. The crop has "ashta'a" when its shoots have come out. al-Akhfash said regarding "sent out its shoot" that it means its tip. This was related by al-Tha'labi from al-Kisa'i. al-Farra' said: "ashta'a al-zar'u" means the crop has put forth its shoots when it has emerged, so it is "mushti'" (sprouting).

The poet said:
"The shoot came out over the face of the earth,
and from the trees the branches of fruit."

al-Zajjaj said: "sent out its shoot" means its growth. It is also said that the *shatʾ* is the thorn of the ear of grain. The Arabs also call it *safâ*, which is the thorn of *bahmâ* [[*bahmâ*: a plant that goats graze on intensely while it is green]], as said by Qutrub. It is also said that it is the ear of grain, so that one grain produces ten, nine, or eight ears; this was said by al-Farra', and al-Mawardi related it.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Dhakwan read "shata'ahu" with a fatha on the ta', and the rest read it with sukun. Anas, Nasr ibn Asim, and Ibn Wathhab read "shatâhu" like "'asâhu." al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "shatahu" without a hamza. All of these are dialectal variants of the same word.

This is a parable God struck for the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, meaning that they would be few at first and then would increase and multiply. When the Prophet ﷺ began calling people to his religion, he was weak, and one person after another answered him until his affair grew strong, like a crop that appears after sowing, weak at first, then growing stronger from state to state until its plant and its shoots become thick. This is among the most accurate parables and the strongest expressions.

Qatada said: the likeness of the companions of Muhammad ﷺ is written in the Gospel: that there will come forth from a people who grow like a crop, who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

﴿So it strengthened it﴾ means it supported, aided, and reinforced it. The shoot strengthened the crop. It is also said the reverse: the crop strengthened the shoot. The common reading is *âzarahu* with the long vowel. Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Haywa, and Humayd ibn Qays read *fa-azarahu* with the short vowel, like *fa'alahu*. But the well-known form is with the long vowel. Imru' al-Qays said:

"In a winding valley, its plants have strengthened the lote-tree,
a march of armies, victorious and defeated."

[[*al-mahniya* (with a light pronunciation): the singular of *al-mahânî*, which are the bends of valleys. *al-Dâll* (with a light lam): a *sidr* tree.]]

﴿Then it stood firm upon its stalk﴾ means on its stem, on which it stands and so becomes its stalk. *Al-sûq* is the plural of *al-sâq* (stalk). ﴿It pleases the sowers﴾ means this crop pleases its growers. This is a parable, as we have explained: the crop is Muhammad ﷺ, and the shoot is his Companions, who were few and became many, and weak and became strong, as said by al-Dahhak and others. ﴿That He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾: the *lam* is connected to an omitted element, meaning God did this for Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions so that He might enrage the disbelievers by them.

The fourth concerns God's words: ﴿God has promised those who believe﴾, meaning God promised those who are with Muhammad, namely the believers whose deeds are righteous, ﴿forgiveness and a great reward﴾, that is, a reward that does not end, which is Paradise.

The word "*min*" in His words "*minhum*" [[among them]] does not indicate partiality, singling out some Companions over others. Rather, it is general and specifying the kind, like His words: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [[Qur'an 22:30]]. It does not aim at partiality, but refers to the genus: "avoid the abomination of the kind of idols," since abomination comes in many kinds, among them adultery, usury, drinking wine, and lying. So "*min*" is used here to indicate the genus. Likewise "*minhum*" means "of this kind," that is, the kind of Companions. One says: "Spend your expenditure in dirhams," meaning make your expenditure this kind.

The Companions of Muhammad ﷺ may be singled out for the promise of forgiveness as an honor for them, even though God promises forgiveness to all believers.

There is another answer to the verse: "*min*" here reinforces the statement, and the meaning is "God promised them all forgiveness and a great reward." This follows the pattern of the Arabic saying: "I cut from the cloth a shirt," meaning "I cut the whole cloth into a shirt," where "*min*" did not make any part partial. An example of this in the Qur'an is: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing﴾ [[Qur'an 17:82]]. Its meaning is "We send down the Qur'an as a healing," because every letter of it heals, and healing is not restricted to one part of it over another. Moreover, some linguists say that "*min*" is genus-indicating, its sense being: "We send down healing of the genus of the Qur'an, from the direction of the Qur'an, from the side of the Qur'an." Zuhayr said:

"Is there a dwelling of Umm Awfa that has not been spoken for? [[*al-dimna*: traces of people and what they have blackened with ash. *Lam tukallam*: not made clear. The Arabs say of every trace and other things that have become distinct: *tukallam*, meaning distinguished, so it takes the place of one who speaks.]]"

He meant: from the side of Umm Awfa is a dwelling, or from her dwellings is a dwelling. Another poet said:

"A man of generous gifts, who gives and asks in return,
the lavish one who refuses to be wronged, the carrier of burdens."

Here "*min*" does not make any part partial, since the intended meaning is that he refuses wrongdoing because he is a *nawfal* and a *zafar*. *Al-nawfal* means one who gives much, and *al-zafar* means one who carries the burdens and provisions of people.

The fifth concerns what Abu Urwa al-Zubayri, of the descendants of al-Zubayr, narrated: "We were with Malik ibn Anas, and they mentioned a man who belittled the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Malik recited this verse: 'Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and those with him...' until he reached 'He pleases the sowers, that He may enrage the disbelievers by them.' Then Malik said: whoever among people wakes up with rage in his heart against any of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, this verse has afflicted him." Abu Bakr al-Khatib mentioned it.

I say: Malik has spoken well in his statement and has been correct in his interpretation. Whoever belittles one of them or finds fault with him in his narration has rejected God, Lord of the worlds, and has nullified the laws of the Muslims. God, exalted is He, said: "Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and those with him are harsh against the disbelievers..." to the end of the verse. And He said: ﴿God was well pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾ [[Qur'an 48:18]], along with other verses that contain praise of them and testimony to their truthfulness and success. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with God﴾ [[Qur'an 33:23]]. And He said: "For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their wealth, seeking bounty from God and His good pleasure... to His words... those are the truthful."

[al-Hashr: 8], then the Almighty said: ﴿And those who were settled in the abode and in faith before them... up to His saying... it is they who are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9, note: verse 9 of Surat al-Hashr]. And all of this is with His knowledge, blessed and exalted is He, of their condition and the outcome of their affair.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of people is my generation, then those who follow them." He also said: "Do not revile my Companions. For if one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor even half of it." Both are related by al-Bukhari. In another hadith: "If one of you were to spend what is on the earth, it would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor even half of it."

Abu 'Ubayd said: Its meaning is that it would not reach the mudd of one of them when he gives charity with it, nor half a mudd. Thus, al-nasif here means half. Similarly, one says 'ashir for a tenth, khamis for a fifth, tasi' for a ninth, thamin for an eighth, sabi' for a seventh, sadis for a sixth, and rabi' for a quarter. The Arabs did not say thalith for a third.

In al-Bazzar, from Jabir, with a sound chain traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah chose my Companions above the worlds, apart from the prophets and messengers, and He chose for me four of my Companions, meaning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, and made them my Companions." He also said: "Among all my Companions there is good."

'Uwaym ibn Sa'idah related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, chose me and chose for me my Companions. He made among them for me ministers, in-laws and relatives by marriage. Whoever reviles them, upon him is the curse of Allah, of the angels and of all people, and Allah will not accept from him on the Day of Resurrection any repentance (sarf) or ransom ('adl)." [Al-sarf: repentance. It was said: voluntary worship. Al-'adl: ransom. It was said: obligatory worship.]

The hadiths with this meaning are numerous. Therefore, beware of falling into speaking ill of any one of them, as did the one who attacked the religion by saying that the two Mu'awwidhatayn (the last two surahs, al-Falaq and al-Nas) are not part of the Qur'an. No hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) confirming them and their inclusion in the body of revelation is authentic, except one narrated by 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir. 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir is weak, and no one else agreed with him on it, so his narration is rejected. This is a rejection of what we have mentioned from the Book and the Sunnah, and a nullification of what the Companions have transmitted to us of the religion. For 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir ibn 'Abs al-Juhani is among those who transmitted the Sharia to us in the Sahihayn of al-Bukhari and Muslim and elsewhere. He is among those whom Allah praised, described, commended, and promised forgiveness and a great reward. Whoever attributes to him, or to any one of the Companions, a lie, has left the Sharia, nullified the Qur'an, and slandered the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Whenever any one of them is charged with lying, he is reviled, for after disbelief in Allah there is no greater disgrace or defect than lying. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed whoever reviles his Companions. So whoever calls the least of them a liar (and there is no insignificant one among them) is included in the curse of Allah, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) testified to, and it binds everyone who reviles one of his Companions or slanders him.

'Umar ibn Habib said: I attended the assembly of Harun al-Rashid when a matter arose over which those present disputed and their voices rose. Some of them argued with a hadith related by Abu Hurayrah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Some of them raised the hadith, and the rebuttal and quarrelling increased until some of them said: "This hadith is not accepted as coming from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because Abu Hurayrah is suspect in what he narrates," and they openly called him a liar. I saw al-Rashid inclining toward them and supporting their view. So I said: "The hadith is authentic from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Abu Hurayrah is sound in transmission, truthful in what he narrates from the Prophet (ﷺ) and others." Al-Rashid looked at me with an angry glance, and I rose from the assembly and went home. I had not stayed long when it was said: "The postmaster is at the door." He entered and said to me: "Answer the Commander of the Faithful, answering as one about to be killed, and perform the embalming and shrouding!" I said: "O Allah, You know that I defended the companion of Your Prophet, and I exalted Your Prophet from being slandered through his Companions, so deliver me from him." I was brought before al-Rashid, who was sitting on a golden chair, with his arms bared, the sword in his hand and the leather mat before him. When he saw me he said: "O 'Umar ibn Habib, what did you meet my statement with, in rebuttal and rejection, the same as you met me with?" I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what you said and argued for contains disparagement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of what he brought. If his Companions are liars, then the Sharia is false, and the obligations and rulings concerning fasting, prayer, divorce, marriage and the prescribed punishments are all rejected and unaccepted." He reflected upon himself and then said: "You have revived me, O 'Umar ibn Habib, may Allah revive you!" And he ordered ten thousand dirhams to be given to me.

I said: The Companions are all upright (udul), the friends of Allah the Exalted and His chosen ones, and the best of His creation after His prophets and messengers. This is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah), and what the majority of the imams of this Ummah hold. A small group, which is not to be heeded, has held that the state of the Companions is like the state of others, so their uprightness must be investigated. Some distinguished between their condition at the beginning of the matter, saying: "They were upright at that time, but then their circumstances changed, wars and bloodshed appeared among them, so investigation is necessary." This is rejected, for the best and most excellent of the Companions, such as 'Ali, Talhah, al-Zubayr and others, may Allah be pleased with them, are among those whom Allah praised, purified, was pleased with, and made them pleased, and promised them Paradise through His saying: "forgiveness and a great reward." Especially the ten who were promised Paradise by the report of the Messenger (ﷺ) are the models, despite their knowledge of many trials and events that occurred among them after their Prophet, through his informing them of that. This does not diminish their rank or excellence, since those matters were based on ijtihad (independent reasoning), and every mujtahid is correct. The discussion of those matters will come in Surat al-Hujurat, God willing, in detail.
